This variegated leopard plant selection produces the same bold, glossy, rounded leaves as the species but irregularly splashed and margined in creamy white, brightening deep shade far more than the solid green form, with clusters of daisy-like yellow flowers rising above the foliage in fall. It is a striking accent for a shaded courtyard, bog garden edge, or large container where its coarse, variegated foliage can be appreciated up close, and it pairs well with dark-leaved hostas and ferns. Keep soil consistently moist, since the large leaves wilt quickly in dry conditions, and protect from hard freezes where marginally hardy.

This colorful sport of strawberry begonia forms rounded, scalloped leaves edged in cream and flushed rose-pink, sending out thin red runners tipped with small plantlets in the same strawberry-like fashion as the species, with airy sprays of small white flowers in late spring. Its bright variegation makes it a favorite for shaded hanging baskets, terrariums, and container groundcover where its trailing runners can cascade over an edge. It is slower and less aggressive than the green species, so it rarely becomes a groundcover pest, and benefits from bright indirect light to maintain strong variegation.

Hylomecon japonica is a poppy-family woodland ephemeral from Japan, Korea, and China closely resembling the North American celandine poppy, with soft, deeply divided, fern-like leaves and cheerful, four-petaled, bright yellow flowers held above the foliage in early to mid spring. It spreads gently by rhizome to form a loose colony in humus-rich woodland soil, making an attractive spring companion for trillium, bloodroot, and other woodland ephemerals before going summer-dormant. Give it consistent spring moisture while in growth and avoid disturbing the shallow rhizomes once established.

planting.note: Plant dormant tubers or divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Siberian fumewort is a spring ephemeral that goes fully dormant by early summer, so mark its location to avoid disturbing the dormant tubers later in the season.

directions: Plant dormant tubers or divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Siberian fumewort is a spring ephemeral that goes fully dormant by early summer, so mark its location to avoid disturbing the dormant tubers later in the season. Corydalis ambigua is a diminutive East Asian woodland ephemeral producing finely divided, ferny blue-green foliage and short spikes of vivid sky-blue to purple-blue, spurred flowers in earliest spring, often blooming alongside snowdrops and crocus before the tree canopy leafs out. It naturalizes gently from self-sown seed and offsets in a woodland rock garden or beneath deciduous shrubs, disappearing completely by summer to leave room for later-emerging perennials. Plant it in generous drifts for the best display, since individual plants are small, and avoid summer irrigation over the dormant tubers, which prefer to stay drier once foliage has died back.

Iris gracilipes is a diminutive Japanese and Chinese woodland species with thin, grass-like foliage and slender, branching stems bearing small, delicate, lilac-purple flowers with a crested yellow-and-white signal patch in late spring — remarkably shade-tolerant for an iris, thriving in the dappled light beneath deciduous trees where most iris species would fail to bloom. It spreads slowly to form a dainty clump and is best appreciated up close in a shaded rock garden, trough, or the front of a woodland border alongside other small-scale shade plants like foamflower and dwarf hosta. Keep soil evenly moist through the growing season and divide congested clumps after flowering to maintain vigor.
